prompt: To estimate the mean weekly study hours of all students at a university, a reporter interviews $50$ students in the library at $7$ a.m. on a Monday. How will this sample most likely affect the estimate?

choices.label: It will likely OVERESTIMATE the mean, because early-morning library users study more than typical students
It will likely UNDERESTIMATE the mean, because tired students cannot study well
It will be unbiased, because $50$ students is a large enough sample
It will be unbiased, because the reporter did not choose who would be in the library

hint: This is a convenience sample. Ask how the people in it differ from the population, and in which direction.

hints.text: This is a convenience sample. Ask how the people in it differ from the population, and in which direction.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up: estimating how much people exercise by surveying a gym at 6 a.m. would clearly overestimate. Same reasoning for the library.
Students who are in the library before 8 a.m. on a Monday are probably the heavy studiers. Does that push the sample mean up or down?
The sample is loaded with heavy studiers, so the estimate is too high: choice A.

explanation: Students in the library at 7 a.m. are not typical. They are the ones who study the most, and students who rarely study are almost never there.
A sample that systematically includes high values produces a mean that is too high: the estimate will overstate the true mean.
Choice A. Sample size cannot fix a biased method (C), and "the reporter did not choose" is not the same as random selection (D).

alternativeExplanations.title: Bias is about the method, not luck
steps: Repeat this method every Monday and you would get high estimates again and again.
That consistent lean in one direction is bias; it does not shrink as you add more 7 a.m. library-goers.
Only a random sample of ALL students fixes the lean.

alternativeExplanations.title: The trap in choice D
steps: It is true the reporter did not hand-pick anyone, but the location and time did the picking.
Random sampling means every student had a known chance of selection; a student who never visits the library had zero chance.
Zero chance for part of the population means undercoverage and bias.
